title: Heaps and priority queues
summary: A structure that always hands you the smallest (or most urgent) item next, cheaply, even while new items keep arriving.

sections.heading: What a heap is for
body: Sorting once is fine when all the data is there up front. A heap is for when items keep arriving and you keep asking "what is the smallest now?". Adding an item and taking the smallest both cost O(log n).
- Scheduling: always run the most urgent job next.
- The `k` largest or smallest items of a long stream.
- Shortest paths on weighted graphs (Dijkstra's algorithm).

sections.heading: Using one in Python
body: Python's `heapq` module turns a plain list into a min-heap. Push tuples to give each item a priority: tuples compare by their first element first.

python.code:
import heapq

jobs = []
heapq.heappush(jobs, (3, 'write tests'))
heapq.heappush(jobs, (1, 'fix the outage'))
heapq.heappush(jobs, (2, 'review a change'))
while jobs:
    priority, name = heapq.heappop(jobs)
    print(priority, name)

print(heapq.nlargest(2, [5, 1, 9, 3]))
python.output:
1 fix the outage
2 review a change
3 write tests
[9, 5]

sections.heading: Building one in JavaScript
body: JavaScript has no built-in heap, so here is a small one. It is an array viewed as a tree: the item at index `i` has children at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`, and its parent is at `(i - 1) / 2` rounded down. Every parent is smaller than its children, so the smallest item is always at index 0.
- **push**: add at the end, then swap upwards while smaller than the parent.
- **pop**: take index 0, move the last item to the top, then swap it downwards with its smaller child until it fits.

mistakes: Expecting the heap's array to be fully sorted. Only the first item is guaranteed to be the smallest.
Python's `heapq` is a min-heap only. For a max-heap, push negated priorities.
Sorting the whole list again after every insert, which is O(n log n) each time instead of O(log n).
